subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement best describes the transition elements when they are compared with the Group 1 metals?
items.correct: They have properties that are similar to each other but different from Group 1 metals
items.misconception: They react with water and with oxygen far more violently than Group 1 metals
items.why: In everyday language 'strong' and 'powerful' describe the same thing, and students carry that over into chemistry. The transition metals are also the ones seen doing heavy work in bridges and engines, which reinforces the idea that they are the aggressive ones. Hardness and strength are physical properties; reactivity is a chemical property, and the two are separate. Group 1 metals are soft, weak and extremely reactive, while transition elements are hard, strong and much less reactive.
items.random_wrong: They form only one fixed ion each, just like the Group 1 metals do

items.q: Sodium melts at 98 degrees C and chromium melts at 1907 degrees C. Which conclusion do these values support?
items.correct: Transition elements usually melt at much higher temperatures than Group 1 metals
items.misconception: The sodium sample was impure, because every metal melts well above 1000 degrees C
items.why: The metals students meet in workshops and in industry are steels and copper alloys, all of which need furnace temperatures to melt. Group 1 metals are only ever seen stored under oil, so their low melting points are never experienced directly. Group 1 metals have low melting points, and they fall down the group: lithium 180 degrees C, sodium 98 degrees C, potassium 63 degrees C. Transition elements melt far higher: iron 1538 degrees C and chromium 1907 degrees C.
items.random_wrong: Chromium melts higher because it is the more reactive metal of the two

items.q: A small piece of sodium floats on water, but a small piece of copper sinks. What does this show?
items.correct: Sodium is less dense than water, while copper is far denser than water
items.misconception: Sodium cannot be a true metal, because every metal is denser than water is
items.why: Every metal a student handles day to day is dense, and being heavy is treated as part of the definition of a metal. Density is also often confused with how heavy an object feels rather than mass per unit volume. Group 1 metals have low densities, and lithium, sodium and potassium all float on water. Transition elements are much denser: copper and nickel are both about 8.9 g/cm3 and sink immediately.
items.random_wrong: Sodium melts at a low temperature, so a metal that melts easily is light

items.q: Potassium and nickel are each added to a separate beaker of cold water. What would you see?
items.correct: Potassium fizzes and melts; the nickel does not change
items.misconception: Both metals fizz gently, but the nickel fizzes much more slowly
items.why: The reactivity series is met as a single ranked list, which makes reactivity look like a difference of speed rather than a difference of whether anything happens at all. Rusting is also described as iron reacting with water, so students expect iron and water to react on contact. Group 1 metals react with cold water on contact. Transition elements such as chromium, nickel and copper react extremely slowly or not at all, which is why copper is used for water pipes. Rusting needs water and oxygen together over days, not seconds.
items.random_wrong: Neither metal reacts, because unreactive metals like nickel show no change

items.q: Freshly cut sodium and freshly polished copper are both left out in air. What happens to their shiny surfaces?
items.correct: The sodium dulls within seconds; the copper only dulls slowly over months
items.misconception: The copper stays shiny for ever, because it never reacts with oxygen
items.why: Copper pipes and stainless steel cutlery survive for years, so these metals are experienced as inert. The word 'unreactive' is then treated as an absolute rather than as a comparison with Group 1. Transition elements are less reactive than Group 1 metals, not unreactive. They react with oxygen and with halogens more slowly, and usually need heating, but the reactions do happen.
items.random_wrong: The sodium stays shiny, while the copper dulls in a few seconds

items.q: Sodium and iron are each heated in chlorine gas. Which statement about these two reactions is correct?
items.correct: Sodium reacts violently, while iron reacts less readily to give FeCl3
items.misconception: Iron reacts far more violently, because it is the harder, stronger metal
items.why: In everyday language 'strong' and 'powerful' describe the same thing, and students carry that over into chemistry. The transition metals are also the ones seen doing heavy work in bridges and engines, which reinforces the idea that they are the aggressive ones. Hardness and strength are physical properties; reactivity is a chemical property, and the two are separate. Group 1 metals are soft, weak and extremely reactive, while transition elements are hard, strong and much less reactive.
items.random_wrong: Only sodium reacts, as transition metals never react with halogens

items.q: Element X melts at 1495 degrees C, has a density of 8.9 g/cm3 and shows no reaction with cold water. Which element is X most likely to be?
items.correct: Cobalt, because those values are typical of a transition metal
items.misconception: Sodium, because metals such as sodium melt at above 1000 degrees C
items.why: The metals students meet in workshops and in industry are steels and copper alloys, all of which need furnace temperatures to melt. Group 1 metals are only ever seen stored under oil, so their low melting points are never experienced directly. Group 1 metals have low melting points, and they fall down the group: lithium 180 degrees C, sodium 98 degrees C, potassium 63 degrees C. Transition elements melt far higher: iron 1538 degrees C and chromium 1907 degrees C.
items.random_wrong: Lithium, because all metals are dense and sink in water

items.q: Which set of properties is typical of many of the transition elements?
items.correct: Ions of different charges, coloured compounds, catalysts
items.misconception: One fixed ion charge, white compounds and use as catalysts
items.why: Ionic bonding is taught first with Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7, where the charge is fixed by the group number. That rule is powerful and gets applied to the whole periodic table, including the block where it does not hold. The group-number rule works for the main groups only. Transition elements form ions with different charges, which is why their names carry a Roman numeral: iron(II) and iron(III), copper(I) and copper(II).
items.random_wrong: Ions of different charges, white compounds and low densities

items.q: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue, but sodium sulfate solution is colourless. What is the best explanation?
items.correct: Copper is a transition element, and its compounds are usually coloured
items.misconception: The sulfate ion gives the blue colour in any sulfate solution
items.why: Copper(II) sulfate is the first coloured salt most students meet, and it is met so often that its colour becomes attached to the word 'sulfate'. Names are also read left to right, so the last-named part feels like the important one. In these compounds the colour comes from the transition metal ion. Copper(II) sulfate is blue, iron(II) sulfate is pale green and sodium sulfate is white, yet all three contain the same sulfate ion.
items.random_wrong: Both compounds are colourless, so the blue must come from an impurity

items.q: Iron forms two chlorides, FeCl2 and FeCl3. What does the (II) in the name iron(II) chloride tell you?
items.correct: The iron ion in this compound carries a charge of 2+
items.misconception: Two chlorine atoms are joined to each of the iron atoms
items.why: For iron(II) chloride the numeral and the number of chlorine atoms happen to coincide, so the wrong rule gives the right formula and is never challenged. It then fails on compounds such as manganese(IV) oxide, MnO2. The Roman numeral always gives the charge on the metal ion. Manganese(IV) oxide contains a 4+ manganese ion but only two oxygen atoms, MnO2, which shows that the numeral is not an atom count.
items.random_wrong: The iron atom has lost two protons from the nucleus

items.q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly. When manganese(IV) oxide is added, oxygen is given off quickly. What is the manganese(IV) oxide doing?
items.correct: It speeds up the reaction and is not itself used up
items.misconception: It is used up in the reaction, so more must be added each time
items.why: Anything added to a reaction vessel looks like a reactant, and students see the catalyst mixed in with everything else. Industrial catalysts do have to be replaced eventually, which is often mentioned and then over-generalised. A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up by it. It does not appear in the balanced equation, and it can be recovered unchanged in mass at the end of the reaction.
items.random_wrong: It raises the total volume of oxygen that can be given off

items.q: Sodium can be cut with a knife, but chromium is used for tools and hard-wearing plating. What does this show?
items.correct: Transition elements are hard and strong, while Group 1 metals are soft
items.misconception: Chromium is harder, so it is also the more reactive of the two
items.why: In everyday language 'strong' and 'powerful' describe the same thing, and students carry that over into chemistry. The transition metals are also the ones seen doing heavy work in bridges and engines, which reinforces the idea that they are the aggressive ones. Hardness and strength are physical properties; reactivity is a chemical property, and the two are separate. Group 1 metals are soft, weak and extremely reactive, while transition elements are hard, strong and much less reactive.
items.random_wrong: Sodium is too soft to be counted as a proper metal at all

items.q: Iron forms Fe2+ and Fe3+. Are these two different elements?
items.correct: No. Both are iron, with 26 protons. Fe2+ is an iron atom that has lost two electrons and Fe3+ one that has lost three.
items.misconception: If the charge is different then something in the nucleus must be different, so Fe3+ has a different number of protons from Fe2+.
items.why: Charge is first met when defining protons and electrons, and proton number is stressed as the thing that fixes which element you have. Students then reach for the nucleus whenever a charge changes, instead of for the outer electrons. Ion charge comes from electrons lost or gained; proton number never changes in a chemical reaction. A transition element can lose different numbers of electrons, which is exactly why it forms ions with different charges.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does adding a catalyst increase the mass of product you finally obtain?
items.correct: No. It gets you to the same amount of product faster; the amount made at the end is not increased.
items.misconception: A catalyst improves the reaction, so it must increase how much product you end up with.
items.why: 'Speeds up' and 'improves' merge into one vague idea of making the reaction better, and industrial catalysts are described as making a process more productive, which is about time rather than amount. A catalyst changes the rate only. The amount of product is fixed by the amounts of reactant and by the balanced equation, so a catalyst gets you there sooner, not further.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all metal compounds white solids?
items.correct: No. Group 1 compounds are usually white, but transition metal compounds are usually coloured.
items.misconception: Compounds are white crystals like salt, so transition metal compounds are white too and dissolve to give colourless solutions.
items.why: Sodium chloride is the model compound in almost every lesson on ionic bonding, and the compounds handled in early practical work are mostly white powders, so being white becomes part of what a compound is. Transition metal compounds are usually coloured, both as solids and in solution: copper(II) sulfate blue, nickel(II) sulfate green, iron(III) oxide red-brown, potassium manganate(VII) purple.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Sodium melts easily. Does that also tell you it has a low density?
items.correct: Both happen to be true for sodium, but one does not follow from the other. Melting point and density are separate properties.
items.misconception: A metal that melts at a low temperature must also be a light metal, because melting point and density measure much the same thing.
items.why: Both properties are used to sort metals into 'soft light ones' and 'tough heavy ones', so students bundle them into a single idea instead of treating them as two independent measurements. Density is mass per unit volume; melting point is the temperature at which a solid turns liquid. Mercury has a very low melting point and a very high density, which shows that the two are independent.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Copper metal is red-brown. Should copper(II) sulfate solution be red-brown too?
items.correct: No. Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue, even though the metal it comes from is red-brown.
items.misconception: A compound shows the colour of the metal it is made from, so the colour of the metal tells you the colour of the compound.
items.why: Colour is treated as a fixed possession of a substance rather than a property of the particles present, so it is transferred from element to compound without any expectation that it will change. The colour belongs to the ion, not to the metal. Copper metal is red-brown while copper(II) ions in solution are blue, and iron metal is grey while iron(III) oxide is red-brown.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
